source.title: SEDATE: Do Large Language Models Share an Aggression Circuit Across Languages?
source.authors: Sagnik Basu; Sayan Das; Somnath Banerjee; Animesh Mukherjee

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some table extraction is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops SEDATE as a safety defense, using aggression-sensitive neurons to suppress and redirect generation, and reports how that method performs. It does not test the claim versions about fine-tuning, response-position KL, opening-token bypass, or whether safety behavior is localized in a small parameter set.
record.gate_note: The paper reports multilingual unsafe-rate changes after its own combined intervention. These are results for a defense method, not tests of the claim versions. Its cited statements about refusal directions and safety alignment are prior work, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes SEDATE, an inference-time defense that detects and edits aggression-sensitive FFN neurons, and reports only that method's performance. It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning (V1, V2) and no per-token KL between aligned and base models (V3). It runs no prefill, suffix or decoding attack (V4) and no deepening training (V7). Its neuron selection uses aggression-vs-benign activation entropy, a different construct from safety behaviour carried by few weights. The neurons are found even in base models without safety training. The measured effect also combines attenuation, residual steering and a fixed refusal fallback, so it cannot show localization of safety (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that a cross-lingual shared set of aggression-selective neurons exists, and that SEDATE (detect–edit–verify with refusal fallback) outperforms the unintervened model and baselines across 7 languages and model families. They report that it generalizes to 4 unseen languages and 4 datasets while retaining capability, with summarization (CNN/DM ROUGE) dropping up to about 5 points. They frame the neurons as both detector and intervention target, offering an alternative to retraining-based alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes a training-free, inference-time detect–edit–verify defense using neuron attenuation, residual-stream steering, and fallback refusal; it does not reproduce the claim's original methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported unsafe-rate reductions vary substantially by model and language; reductions are generally larger for base models than instruction-tuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: A cross-lingual core of FFN neurons, selected by low AAPE entropy, fires preferentially on aggressive vs benign text in base and instruct models. Conditionally attenuating them plus residual steering and refusal fallback lowers Llama Guard 3 unsafe rates by 28–56 points on base models and 1–40 points on instruct models (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm-content-selective neurons shared across languages can serve as a detector and intervention target to reduce unsafe generations at inference time.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the unsafe-rate differences in Table 7. The reported safety intervention combines neuron attenuation, residual-stream steering, and a refusal fallback, so its effects do not isolate the contribution of the neuron set alone. The paper gives no exact unmodified unsafe rates in Table 7.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, retained all 49 language-by-model unsafe-rate results from Appendix E, Table 7. Did not extract the separate cost-per-token results in Table 1, human comparisons in Table 4, LLM-judge comparisons in Appendix D, or capability benchmark values in Table 5; these are additional evaluations of the defense, not claim-version tests.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples and no compliance measurement after it.
No per-position KL or token-depth analysis of aligned vs base models.
No prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding-change attacks.

Aggression-selective neurons are identified, but there is no test that safety behaviour of aligned models resides in a small weight or rank set. No ablation of the neurons alone is reported to raise or lower refusal.
No analysis of whether data or objective causes shallow alignment.
No training that spreads safety across positions; SEDATE is training-free and not evaluated against attacks that would test depth.

record.verdict_notes: All 49 rows are the study's own defense results and carry no version link; their observed/partial states describe method effect size, not a claim version. Section 5.2 lists three model families, but results include Aya-instruct (aya-expanse-8b). Table 7 gives deltas only, with no absolute unintervened unsafe rates and no uncertainty. The paper cites Qi et al. 2024 (HEx-PHI, an original source) only as an OOD dataset.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning or resulting refusal/compliance measurement.
No benign-data fine-tuning or resulting harmful-compliance measurement.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change bypass test.
The paper identifies and edits aggression-sensitive neurons, but does not isolate whether safety behavior is carried by a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether training data or objective produces shallow safety.
No training that deepens safety across response positions or evaluation of whether such training holds up.
